# Site Prompt

Produce one markdown file that a code generator can paste into an empty directory to rebuild a website exactly. The prompt is the deliverable; the site built along the way is scaffolding. Every claim in the prompt must have been run.

## Own the prompt, not the site

- **In:** a topic, optionally with a brand, name, domain, audience, must-have content or stack constraints.
- **Out:** `site-prompts/<slug>.md` in the current project, or the path the user names. One file.
- **Stop at the prompt.** An actual build goes to `sites-building`; hosting to `sites-hosting`; critique of an existing page to `impeccable` or `frontend-design`; skill authoring to `draft-skill`.

## The subject is the concept

A topic is not a theme. "Ship" is a category, and a site about "ships" is a template with nautical nouns. Narrow it to one concrete subject, one audience and one job, then derive the page from that subject's world. SELENE is not a reusable template: its Earthrise, trajectory and mission reel exist because the subject is a lunar voyage. A cargo ship site must earn its own sections, vocabulary and signature interaction.

Before designing, fill in the brief in `references/subject-brief.md`:

- one concrete subject, not a category;
- audience, and the job the page does for them;
- the single job of the page;
- at least eight terms a practitioner actually uses, plus the artifact world;
- one signature mechanic only this subject would earn;
- the tension the page dramatizes;
- what can be claimed honestly.

One ambiguous word ("ship") is not a brief. Pick the most commercial reading, state the assumption in the prompt, and proceed. Ask only when the fork changes a claim, such as a real operator versus a concept or a regulated service.

Run the swap test before building: replace the subject with something unrelated. If the sections, motion and copy still work, the concept is templated; redesign. `references/subject-brief.md` has worked SELENE and cargo-ship derivations and the template-smell list.

## Workflow

1. Fill the subject brief. Do not design yet.
2. Choose the smallest stack that serves the concept; read `references/stack-presets.md`.
   - Static HTML, CSS and JS when content plus light interaction is all the page needs.
   - Vite + React + TS + Tailwind only when scroll choreography, shared state or a component system is load-bearing.
   - If the site needs auth, payments, a database or a live AI backend, stop: this skill writes marketing and concept sites, not products.
3. Build the real site in a temp directory outside the project. Write final copy first, then layout, then motion. No lorem ipsum, placeholder images or hotlinked stock.
4. Swap-test again. Cut every section that would survive a topic change.
5. Verify with `references/verification.md`. Record which checks ran, at which viewports, and which did not run.
6. Write the prompt using `references/prompt-format.md`. Every file appears in full under a `## File:` heading. No ellipses, no "same as above", no scratch paths, no localhost.
7. Replay-test the prompt:

       node scripts/replay-prompt.mjs <prompt.md> --out <clean-dir>
       node scripts/replay-prompt.mjs <prompt.md> --check <built-dir>

   Then build the replay directory. Every file must match and the build must pass. If not, the prompt is not done.
8. Report the prompt path, narrowed subject, stack, file count, checks run and not run, replay result, and any prompt inconsistency left in the source.

Trigger cases for this skill live in `tests/trigger-cases.md`; the verifier's own cases are in `tests/replay-cases.md`. The trigger cases are specification until they are run.

## Keep the prompt honest

- The receiver has never seen this conversation. Any sentence pointing at the scratch build, the design discussion or the generator breaks it.
- Never write a check into the prompt that was not run. The "Checks already run" section lists commands, viewports, results and the unverified remainder.
- Visuals are code-native: SVG, CSS, canvas, gradients, inline data URIs. No remote images or asset hotlinks. Google Fonts links are allowed; other third-party URLs are not. User-supplied images are external inputs; say exactly where they must be placed.
- Do not carry SELENE's layer stack, mission reel, trajectory or countdown into another topic. Reuse a mechanic only when the subject earns it.
- Mark invented operators, lines and missions as concepts. Do not invent customers, logos, certifications, ratings or performance metrics.
- Keep comments that record why a number has its value; the receiver will otherwise "fix" it.
- The negative rules in the prompt ("do not improve", "do not substitute", "do not add files") are part of the contract, not decoration.

## Hand off

- Actual build or hosting of the generated site: `sites-building`, then `sites-hosting`.
- Critique or redesign of an existing page: `impeccable` or `frontend-design`.
- A batch of prompts to turn into a skill: `prompts-to-skill`.
- Repo naming, description and listing for a published prompt library: `findable`.

# Subject brief and swap test

The brief is the difference between a subject-tailored site and a template with the nouns changed. Fill it before naming colours, sections or motion.

## Brief template

| Field | What goes in it | Bad | Good (cargo ship) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Subject | One concrete instance, not a category | "shipping" | A fictional container liner on one Asia–Europe rotation |
| Audience | Who the page serves and what they already know | "everyone" | Freight forwarders booking 40ft containers |
| Job | The one thing the page must let them do | "learn about us" | Get a quote for a named sailing, or follow one container |
| Vocabulary | At least eight terms a practitioner uses | "cargo" | TEU, deadweight, draft, berth, port rotation, bill of lading, manifest, demurrage, transshipment, cut-off, stevedore |
| Artifacts | The forms and objects of the world | "photos" | Manifest, bill of lading, port rotation, stowage plan, tide table, AIS track |
| Signature mechanic | One interaction only this subject earns | "scroll animations" | The route inks port by port; the selected container advances and the cut-off counts down |
| Tension | What the page dramatizes or argues | "we are the best" | Most cargo is invisible; the page makes one box legible |
| Honest claims | What can be said, and what must be labelled | "99.9% on time" | Fictional line; schedule illustrative; no performance metrics |

## Worked example: SELENE (lunar expedition)

- **Subject:** a concept lunar expedition operator running six to twenty-eight day trips.
- **Audience:** affluent experience-seekers.
- **Job:** put a name on the manifest.
- **Vocabulary:** translunar injection, lunar orbit insertion, regolith, Mare Tranquillitatis, mission clock, launch window.
- **Artifacts:** mission log, trajectory, mission classes, launch-window countdown, manifest form.
- **Signature mechanic:** a scroll-driven Earthrise cut into six photographic layers, then an Earth-to-Moon route that inks itself leg by leg.
- **Tension:** the first holiday that leaves the planet.
- **Sections earned:** Earthrise, mission log, trajectory, mission classes, reserve. Every one has a subject reason.
- **Sections not earned:** SaaS pricing tiers, a customer-logo wall, a blog grid. They would survive a topic swap.

## Worked example: cargo ship (container liner)

- **Subject:** a fictional container line on one Asia–Europe rotation, for example Shanghai, Singapore, Suez, Rotterdam, Felixstowe.
- **Audience:** freight forwarders and small shippers comparing sailings.
- **Job:** request a quote for a named sailing, or follow one container.
- **Vocabulary:** TEU, deadweight, draft, berth, port rotation, bill of lading, manifest, demurrage, transshipment, cut-off, tide window, stevedore.
- **Visual world:** marine chart lines and soundings, container livery, oxidized steel, stencil lettering, port timestamps, tide tables. Palette: deep sea black, signal orange, salt white, rust. Type: condensed industrial sans for display, humanist sans for text, mono for the port log.
- **Signature mechanic:** the page follows one container from berth to berth. A chart-like route inks leg by leg; the current port and cut-off countdown are functions of the same scroll progress. Alternative: an inspectable stowage plan. Pick one, not both.
- **Tension:** the network that moves most of what we own is invisible; the page makes one box legible.
- **Sections earned:** a hero naming one sailing; the port rotation; the manifest of one container; the vessel (capacity, draft, berths); a quote form tied to a cut-off.
- **Sections not earned:** a "features" card grid, a "trusted by" logo wall, generic testimonials. They are not of the subject.

### Contrast

| Question | SELENE | Cargo ship |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hero | The Earth rising over the Moon | A named sailing leaving a berth, or a route chart |
| Motion | Dust clears, the Earth climbs | The route inks, the container advances, the cut-off ticks |
| Proof | Mission classes and a drawn trajectory | The rotation, vessel specs and a manifest |
| Form | Add me to the manifest | Quote against a sailing cut-off |
| Carry-over | Its own scroll loop | None of SELENE's mechanics |

## Swap test

1. Replace the subject with something unrelated, for example a coffee subscription.
2. Keep every section, transition and line of copy.
3. If more than a little survives unchanged, the concept is templated. Cut or redesign the parts that survive.
4. Read the vocabulary: would a practitioner recognize their world, or only the nouns?
5. Test the signature mechanic: could it belong to another subject? If yes, it is not a signature.
6. Test the hero: if the headline could be swapped with another industry's, it says nothing.

Run the swap test twice: once after the brief and once after the build. The second run catches drift introduced by implementation.

## Template smells

- Hero = eyebrow + large headline + subhead + two CTAs + gradient.
- Three feature cards with generic icons.
- A "trusted by" wall of invented or unrelated logos.
- Scroll reveals on every section, regardless of meaning.
- Stock photography standing in for the subject.
- Copy that survives any industry: empower, seamless, next-gen, revolutionize, unlock.
- Invented metrics, testimonials, certifications or ratings.
- Reusing the previous site's mechanics because they worked once.

## One-word topics

Treat a single word as a category, not a subject.

- **ship** → for a commercial B2B page, narrow to a container liner or shipbroker; for consumer travel, a ferry route. State the choice and why in the prompt's brief.
- **coffee** → a single roaster, a farm, a subscription, or a cafe. Choose one, with its own ritual and artifacts.
- **fitness** → a coaching practice, a gym, an app. Each earns different sections.

If the user later names a different concrete subject ("ferry", not "container liner"), redesign the concept. A find-and-replace is a failed pass.

## Copy rules

- Write final copy, no lorem ipsum and no bracketed placeholders.
- Use specific nouns and named places; label illustrative dates, prices and schedules.
- Match the subject's voice: a manifest reads like a manifest, a charter quote like a quote.
- Use at least eight subject terms naturally. Do not stuff keywords into headings.
- Make no claim the operator could not defend. When in doubt, mark it as a concept.
# Stack presets

Pick the smallest stack that can carry the page's load-bearing mechanic. A page that scrolls one pinned scene does not need a router; a single-page brochure does not need a build step. Bigger stacks cost the reader more tokens and add failure points the prompt has to describe.

## Static preset

Use when the page is genuinely static: no shared component state, no client routing, no build-time data. One `index.html`, one `styles.css`, one `main.js`. No package manager, no install step.

    ## Tech stack
    Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No framework, no build step, no dependencies.
    Files: index.html, styles.css, main.js.
    Open index.html directly, or serve with `python -m http.server 8080`.

Rules:
- CSS custom properties for the palette and type scale; no preprocessor.
- `requestAnimationFrame` + scroll listeners for motion; no animation library.
- ES modules via `<script type="module" src="main.js">`.
- No CDN scripts and no library links. A Google Fonts stylesheet (with `preconnect`) is the one allowed external request; otherwise use a system stack.

Do not use the static preset for scroll-pinned multi-scene pages, canvas work, or anything that needs component reuse. The hand-written scene state gets unreadable and the "exactly" promise stops meaning anything.

## Vite preset (tested)

Use for a one-page site with several scroll scenes, shared state, or reusable components. These are the versions that were installed and built in the SELENE run, not the ranges that happen to be latest:

| Package | Version |
| --- | --- |
| react | 19.3.1 |
| react-dom | 19.3.1 |
| typescript | 5.8.3 |
| vite | 6.4.4 |
| @vitejs/plugin-react | 5.2.0 |
| tailwindcss | 4.3.3 |
| @tailwindcss/vite | 4.3.3 |
| @types/react | 19.3.0 |
| @types/react-dom | 19.3.0 |
| lenis | 1.3.27 (only when smooth scroll is part of the mechanic) |

In `package.json`, pin with carets for minors and a tilde for TypeScript, as the SELENE prompt does (`^19.1.0`, `~5.8.2`, `^6.2.3`, …). The prompt must state the versions that were actually resolved, because a reader installing today gets whatever the carets allow.

Scripts:

    "dev": "vite --port=3006 --host=0.0.0.0",
    "build": "vite build",
    "preview": "vite preview --port=3006",
    "lint": "tsc --noEmit"

Rules:
- Tailwind v4 through `@tailwindcss/vite`; theme tokens in `@theme` inside `src/index.css`. No `tailwind.config.js` unless a plugin needs one.
- TypeScript strict. `npm run lint` is the type check; there is no ESLint layer unless the prompt includes one.
- One rAF loop owns scroll-driven style writes. Do not mix `useEffect` scroll listeners with the loop for the same elements; that is how two writers fight over one transform.
- `lenis` only if the page needs smooth scrolling for a pinned scene. If it is in `package.json`, it is used.
- No animation library, no icon set, no component library unless the mechanic needs it. SVG drawn inline, icons drawn as SVG.
- Code-split below-the-fold scenes with `React.lazy` only when the build makes the initial bundle genuinely heavy. The SELENE prompt splits six components; a smaller page should not.

## Asset rule for both presets

Every visual is code-native (CSS gradients, SVG, canvas) or a real asset the user supplied. The prompt lists each supplied asset with its path and role. It never contains a hotlink, a signed download URL, or an instruction to fetch from a storage bucket: those expire and the prompt stops building. The single exception is the Google Fonts stylesheet above, which is stable and named in the stack section.
# Verification

The prompt may only list checks that were run against a real build in a real browser. A prompt that claims a clean console when nobody opened the console is worse than one that says "not verified", because the reader stops looking.

## 1. Build the site before writing the prompt

Create a scratch folder outside the repo, write the site there, and run it. This is the source of truth for every file section.

    npm install        # no lockfile commit unless the prompt includes it
    npm run lint       # tsc --noEmit
    npm run build      # production build, zero warnings that matter

Record the resolved versions from `node_modules` or `npm ls --depth=0`, not only the ranges in `package.json`.

## 2. Serve it and read the banner

    npm run dev -- --port=<free-port>
    npm run preview -- --port=<free-port>

Read the port from the server's own banner. Do not assume: port 3000 and 127.0.0.1:3000 can belong to someone else's process, and a bare HTTP 200 is not proof it is yours. Check the title or a known string in the response.

If Vite binds `[::1]`, `curl http://127.0.0.1:<port>` fails with exit 7; use `http://localhost:<port>`. Use user-level tooling (Playwright MCP or equivalent) to load the page.

## 3. Console and network

- No console errors after full page load and scroll. A missing favicon is a real 404; either add the favicon or list it as not verified.
- No failed network requests for assets the prompt lists.
- Every image resolves: scroll the whole page once so lazy images load, then count `img` elements with `naturalWidth === 0`. Expect zero.

## 4. Layout at four widths

Check 390×844, 768×1024, 1280×800, 1920×1080. At each width:

- `document.documentElement.scrollWidth <= document.documentElement.clientWidth` (no horizontal scroll).
- Nav, hero, the signature scene and the final CTA are on screen and readable.
- Mobile menu (if any) opens, navigates to its target, and closes.

Screenshots are useful but do not replace the measurements; some environments do not paint. Read the DOM and computed styles when a screenshot is blank.

## 5. The behaviours the prompt claims

For each load-bearing behaviour in "How the page works", measure it rather than eyeballing it:

- **Scroll scenes.** Sample progress `p` through the scene and read the computed transforms/opacities. Confirm the start state, the end state, and that the middle is monotonic where the prompt says it is.
- **Horizontal reel or pinned section.** Confirm the nearest card to the focus point has the highest opacity and the counter matches it. Confirm the section releases afterwards.
- **Drawn routes or counters.** Confirm the final value equals the data in `content.ts`, not a hard-coded duplicate.
- **Forms.** Submit empty: the invalid message appears and focus moves to the field. Submit valid: the success state appears. Confirm the mailto or endpoint the prompt describes.
- **Countdowns and clocks.** Let one tick and confirm the value changed in the expected direction.

If the prompt makes a claim about order ("dust clears before the Earth rises"), verify the order from the sampled values. If the source does not match the claim, either change the source or change the claim; do not ship the mismatch. Minor mismatches that are part of the design's feel can stay if they are reported honestly.

## 6. Reduced motion

Emulate `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` and reload. The smooth scroll loop is off, decorative bounce loops are off, and every scene still resolves to a readable state (no section stuck at opacity 0, no transform at its start value forever). Scroll-triggered reveals must still fire, immediately.

## 7. Accessibility smoke

- One `h1`; heading levels in order.
- Every image has `alt`, including empty `alt=""` for decorative ones.
- Buttons and links have discernible names; icon-only controls have `aria-label`.
- Focus is visible on the primary CTA and form fields.
- Colour contrast of body text against its background passes 4.5:1 (and 3:1 for large display text).

## 8. Replay the prompt

This is the check specific to this skill. Run

    node scripts/replay-prompt.mjs <prompt.md> --out <fresh-dir>
    node scripts/replay-prompt.mjs <prompt.md> --check <scratch-dir>

`--check` compares every file section against the scratch build, line-endings normalized. Any drift means the prompt does not reproduce the site it claims to reproduce. Then build the replay folder and confirm lint/build pass there too; a byte-identical tree can still fail if the prompt omitted an asset instruction.

## What to write in the prompt

Under "Checks already run" list the checks with results, e.g.:

- `npm run lint` and `npm run build` pass on the versions listed above.
- No horizontal overflow at 390, 768, 1280, 1920.
- All scenes sampled and end states confirmed.
- Reduced motion: loop off, scenes resolve.
- Replay from the file sections produces a byte-identical tree and builds.

Under "Not verified" be specific: a first-run install today, a browser you did not open, an asset not downloaded, a claim in the design notes that is descriptive rather than tested. Honesty here is what makes the rest of the prompt credible.
# Prompt format

The output is one markdown document the user can paste into a fresh agent session. It has to be enough on its own: no links to this skill, no reference to the scratch folder, no "see the files I made".

## Section order

Use these headings in this order. Skip none of them; a prompt without the file sections is a brief, not a one-shot prompt.

1. **Title** — the subject, then a line stating it is a single self-contained prompt and the agent must build the whole site from it.
2. **What this project is** — two or three sentences: product, audience, the page's one job, the setting. Say it is a landing page and what it must make the visitor do (reserve, request a quote, book).
3. **How the page works** — the 3–5 load-bearing behaviours (scroll model, signature mechanic, what the page must show rather than claim), with the contract each one has to satisfy.
4. **Build this exactly** — a short list of hard constraints. For a rebuild of an existing site this says "Reproduce this exactly"; for an original this says "Build this exactly". Either way it rules out substitutes, lookalike assets, added dependencies, and omissions.
5. **Tech stack** — the pinned stack from `references/stack-presets.md`, with exact versions and the commands that were run.
6. **Assets** — either "everything is code-native, generate it in CSS/SVG" or the user-supplied asset list with how each is produced or placed. No hotlinks, no stock-photo placeholders, no referenced URL that will disappear.
7. **Steps to build** — the order to create files, install, and run; the verify commands; what "done" looks like.
8. **File sections** — one `## File: \`path\`` heading per file, each containing exactly one fenced code block with the complete file. This is the part that makes the prompt work.
9. **Design notes** — why the page looks the way it does: palette intent, type pairing, the subject-native details. This is judgement, not a second implementation; no file content should change to "improve" it.
10. **Checks already run** — the checks from `references/verification.md` that were actually run, with their results. Anything not run goes in a short "not verified" list.

## File heading contract

The file sections are parsed by `scripts/replay-prompt.mjs`. They must be exactly:

    ## File: `src/App.tsx`

- Path relative to the project root, forward slashes only, no leading `./`.
- One fenced code block directly under the heading, labelled with the language.
- The block holds the complete file. No `...`, no `// rest of file`, no elisions, no patch hunks.
- No duplicate paths.
- Order: config and entry first (`package.json`, `vite.config.ts`, `tsconfig.json`, `index.html`), then app entry and styles, then data/content, then lib and hooks, then components. That order makes the replay diff readable and the code block sane to read in one pass.
- Images go in the Assets section as instructions. Binary files never appear in a code block.

## The skeleton

    # {Subject} — one-shot build prompt

    This is a single, self-contained prompt. Build the whole site from it. Do not ask questions, do not substitute assets, do not stop until `npm run build` passes.

    ## What this project is
    ...

    ## How the page works
    ...

    ## Build this exactly
    - ...

    ## Tech stack
    ...

    ## Assets
    ...

    ## Steps to build
    ...

    ## File: `package.json`
    ```json
    ...
    ```

    ## File: `index.html`
    ```html
    ...
    ```

    ## Design notes
    ...

    ## Checks already run
    ...

## Things that break a one-shot prompt

- **Placeholders.** "Style this section" or "add your copy here" guarantees an agent will invent generic copy. Write the final copy in the files.
- **Scratch references.** `localhost:4317`, absolute paths from your machine, "the version I tested" without the version number. The prompt travels; those do not.
- **A file list without file bodies.** A file inventory is a brief. Every listed path gets a section, or the path does not get listed.
- **Unverifiable checks.** Listing `npm run lint` as "passing" when it was never run. If you did not run it, move it to "not verified".
- **Commented-out code and TODOs.** They read as unfinished and agents act on them.
- **Leftover subject matter.** A mission-control string in a freight page is a bug in the concept. Run the swap test before you write the sections.
- **An explanation of the skill.** The prompt is for the builder, not a note to the user about how it was made.

2. Keep every section, transition and line of copy.
3. If more than a little survives unchanged, the concept is templated. Cut or redesign the parts that survive.
4. Read the vocabulary: would a practitioner recognize their world, or only the nouns?
5. Test the signature mechanic: could it belong to another subject? If yes, it is not a signature.
6. Test the hero: if the headline could be swapped with another industry's, it says nothing.

Run the swap test twice: once after the brief and once after the build. The second run catches drift introduced by implementation.

## Template smells

- Hero = eyebrow + large headline + subhead + two CTAs + gradient.
- Three feature cards with generic icons.
- A "trusted by" wall of invented or unrelated logos.
- Scroll reveals on every section, regardless of meaning.
- Stock photography standing in for the subject.
- Copy that survives any industry: empower, seamless, next-gen, revolutionize, unlock.
- Invented metrics, testimonials, certifications or ratings.
- Reusing the previous site's mechanics because they worked once.

## One-word topics

Treat a single word as a category, not a subject.

- **ship** → for a commercial B2B page, narrow to a container liner or shipbroker; for consumer travel, a ferry route. State the choice and why in the prompt's brief.
- **coffee** → a single roaster, a farm, a subscription, or a cafe. Choose one, with its own ritual and artifacts.
- **fitness** → a coaching practice, a gym, an app. Each earns different sections.

If the user later names a different concrete subject ("ferry", not "container liner"), redesign the concept. A find-and-replace is a failed pass.

## Copy rules

- Write final copy, no lorem ipsum and no bracketed placeholders.
- Use specific nouns and named places; label illustrative dates, prices and schedules.
- Match the subject's voice: a manifest reads like a manifest, a charter quote like a quote.
- Use at least eight subject terms naturally. Do not stuff keywords into headings.
- Make no claim the operator could not defend. When in doubt, mark it as a concept.
# Stack presets

Pick the smallest stack that can carry the page's load-bearing mechanic. A page that scrolls one pinned scene does not need a router; a single-page brochure does not need a build step. Bigger stacks cost the reader more tokens and add failure points the prompt has to describe.

## Static preset

Use when the page is genuinely static: no shared component state, no client routing, no build-time data. One `index.html`, one `styles.css`, one `main.js`. No package manager, no install step.

    ## Tech stack
    Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No framework, no build step, no dependencies.
    Files: index.html, styles.css, main.js.
    Open index.html directly, or serve with `python -m http.server 8080`.

Rules:
- CSS custom properties for the palette and type scale; no preprocessor.
- `requestAnimationFrame` + scroll listeners for motion; no animation library.
- ES modules via `<script type="module" src="main.js">`.
- No CDN scripts and no library links. A Google Fonts stylesheet (with `preconnect`) is the one allowed external request; otherwise use a system stack.

Do not use the static preset for scroll-pinned multi-scene pages, canvas work, or anything that needs component reuse. The hand-written scene state gets unreadable and the "exactly" promise stops meaning anything.

    "preview": "vite preview --port=3006",

- No animation library, no icon set, no component library unless the mechanic needs it. SVG drawn inline, icons drawn as SVG.

Every visual is code-native (CSS gradients, SVG, canvas) or a real asset the user supplied. The prompt lists each supplied asset with its path and role. It never contains a hotlink, a signed download URL, or an instruction to fetch from a storage bucket: those expire and the prompt stops building. The single exception is the Google Fonts stylesheet above, which is stable and named in the stack section.

Create a scratch folder outside the repo, write the site there, and run it. This is the source of truth for every file section.

    npm install        # no lockfile commit unless the prompt includes it
    npm run lint       # tsc --noEmit
    npm run build      # production build, zero warnings that matter

Record the resolved versions from `node_modules` or `npm ls --depth=0`, not only the ranges in `package.json`.

## 2. Serve it and read the banner

    npm run dev -- --port=<free-port>
    npm run preview -- --port=<free-port>

Read the port from the server's own banner. Do not assume: port 3000 and 127.0.0.1:3000 can belong to someone else's process, and a bare HTTP 200 is not proof it is yours. Check the title or a known string in the response.

If Vite binds `[::1]`, `curl http://127.0.0.1:<port>` fails with exit 7; use `http://localhost:<port>`. Use user-level tooling (Playwright MCP or equivalent) to load the page.

## 3. Console and network

- No console errors after full page load and scroll. A missing favicon is a real 404; either add the favicon or list it as not verified.
- No failed network requests for assets the prompt lists.
- Every image resolves: scroll the whole page once so lazy images load, then count `img` elements with `naturalWidth === 0`. Expect zero.

## 4. Layout at four widths

Check 390×844, 768×1024, 1280×800, 1920×1080. At each width:

- `document.documentElement.scrollWidth <= document.documentElement.clientWidth` (no horizontal scroll).
- Nav, hero, the signature scene and the final CTA are on screen and readable.
- Mobile menu (if any) opens, navigates to its target, and closes.

Screenshots are useful but do not replace the measurements; some environments do not paint. Read the DOM and computed styles when a screenshot is blank.

- **Horizontal reel or pinned section.** Confirm the nearest card to the focus point has the highest opacity and the counter matches it. Confirm the section releases afterwards.
- **Drawn routes or counters.** Confirm the final value equals the data in `content.ts`, not a hard-coded duplicate.
- **Forms.** Submit empty: the invalid message appears and focus moves to the field. Submit valid: the success state appears. Confirm the mailto or endpoint the prompt describes.
- **Countdowns and clocks.** Let one tick and confirm the value changed in the expected direction.

If the source does not match the claim, either change the source or change the claim; do not ship the mismatch. Minor mismatches that are part of the design's feel can stay if they are reported honestly.

## 6. Reduced motion

Emulate `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` and reload. The smooth scroll loop is off, decorative bounce loops are off, and every scene still resolves to a readable state (no section stuck at opacity 0, no transform at its start value forever). Scroll-triggered reveals must still fire, immediately.

## 7. Accessibility smoke

- One `h1`; heading levels in order.
- Every image has `alt`, including empty `alt=""` for decorative ones.
- Buttons and links have discernible names; icon-only controls have `aria-label`.
- Focus is visible on the primary CTA and form fields.
- Colour contrast of body text against its background passes 4.5:1 (and 3:1 for large display text).

## 8. Replay the prompt

This is the check specific to this skill. Run

    node scripts/replay-prompt.mjs <prompt.md> --out <fresh-dir>
    node scripts/replay-prompt.mjs <prompt.md> --check <scratch-dir>

`--check` compares every file section against the scratch build, line-endings normalized. Any drift means the prompt does not reproduce the site it claims to reproduce. ## What to write in the prompt

Under "Checks already run" list the checks with results, e.g.:

- `npm run lint` and `npm run build` pass on the versions listed above.
- No horizontal overflow at 390, 768, 1280, 1920.
- All scenes sampled and end states confirmed.
- Reduced motion: loop off, scenes resolve.
- Replay from the file sections produces a byte-identical tree and builds.

Under "Not verified" be specific: a first-run install today, a browser you did not open, an asset not downloaded, a claim in the design notes that is descriptive rather than tested. Honesty here is what makes the rest of the prompt credible.
# Prompt format

The output is one markdown document the user can paste into a fresh agent session. It has to be enough on its own: no links to this skill, no reference to the scratch folder, no "see the files I made".

## Section order

Use these headings in this order. Skip none of them; a prompt without the file sections is a brief, not a one-shot prompt.

1. **Title** — the subject, then a line stating it is a single self-contained prompt and the agent must build the whole site from it.
2. **What this project is** — two or three sentences: product, audience, the page's one job, the setting. Say it is a landing page and what it must make the visitor do (reserve, request a quote, book).
3. **How the page works** — the 3–5 load-bearing behaviours (scroll model, signature mechanic, what the page must show rather than claim), with the contract each one has to satisfy.
4. **Build this exactly** — a short list of hard constraints. For a rebuild of an existing site this says "Reproduce this exactly"; for an original this says "Build this exactly". Either way it rules out substitutes, lookalike assets, added dependencies, and omissions.
5. **Tech stack** — the pinned stack from `references/stack-presets.md`, with exact versions and the commands that were run.
6. **Assets** — either "everything is code-native, generate it in CSS/SVG" or the user-supplied asset list with how each is produced or placed. No hotlinks, no stock-photo placeholders, no referenced URL that will disappear.
7. **Steps to build** — the order to create files, install, and run; the verify commands; what "done" looks like.
8. **File sections** — one `## File: \`path\`` heading per file, each containing exactly one fenced code block with the complete file. This is the part that makes the prompt work.
9. **Design notes** — why the page looks the way it does: palette intent, type pairing, the subject-native details. This is judgement, not a second implementation; no file content should change to "improve" it.
10. **Checks already run** — the checks from `references/verification.md` that were actually run, with their results. Anything not run goes in a short "not verified" list.

## File heading contract

The file sections are parsed by `scripts/replay-prompt.mjs`. They must be exactly:

    ## File: `src/App.tsx`

- Path relative to the project root, forward slashes only, no leading `./`.
- One fenced code block directly under the heading, labelled with the language.
- The block holds the complete file. No `...`, no `// rest of file`, no elisions, no patch hunks.
- No duplicate paths.
- Order: config and entry first (`package.json`, `vite.config.ts`, `tsconfig.json`, `index.html`), then app entry and styles, then data/content, then lib and hooks, then components. That order makes the replay diff readable and the code block sane to read in one pass.
- Images go in the Assets section as instructions. Binary files never appear in a code block.

    # {Subject} — one-shot build prompt

    This is a single, self-contained prompt. Build the whole site from it. Do not ask questions, do not substitute assets, do not stop until `npm run build` passes.

    ## What this project is
    ...

    ## How the page works
    ...

    ## Build this exactly
    - ...

    ## Tech stack
    ...

    ## Assets
    ...

    ## Steps to build
    ...

    ## File: `package.json`
    ```json
    ...
    ```

    ## File: `index.html`
    ```html
    ...
    ```

    ## Design notes
    ...

    ## Checks already run
    ...

- **Placeholders.** "Style this section" or "add your copy here" guarantees an agent will invent generic copy. Write the final copy in the files.
- **Scratch references.** `localhost:4317`, absolute paths from your machine, "the version I tested" without the version number. The prompt travels; those do not.
- **A file list without file bodies.** A file inventory is a brief. Every listed path gets a section, or the path does not get listed.
- **Unverifiable checks.** Listing `npm run lint` as "passing" when it was never run. If you did not run it, move it to "not verified".
- **Commented-out code and TODOs.** They read as unfinished and agents act on them.
- **Leftover subject matter.** A mission-control string in a freight page is a bug in the concept. Run the swap test before you write the sections.
- **An explanation of the skill.** The prompt is for the builder, not a note to the user about how it was made.

I saved the prompt as `site-prompt.md` in the project folder, but I haven't tested any of it. The Bash tool was denied partway through, so I couldn't open the page or run the replay script that compares the prompt's file sections against the site. The prompt's "Checks already run" section says "None", and "Not verified" lists every check I skipped. The code may have bugs that a first browser load would catch.

- **Shop:** "Tannery Row Cycles", a made-up independent workshop in Kirkstall, Leeds. You didn't name a shop, so I invented one and labelled it a concept on the page. The name, address, hours and prices are all illustrative.
- **Placeholder contact details:** the phone number is in the UK range reserved for drama use (0113 496 0142), and the email is on `example.com`. Swap in your real details before using it.
- **Stack:** plain HTML, CSS and JS in three files (`index.html`, `styles.css`, `main.js`). There's no build step or dependencies, and the only external request is Google Fonts.
- **Opening hours:** an "open now / opens tomorrow at 08:00" line in the hero, worked out in Leeds time. It reads from the hours table, so that table is the only place to change them.
- **Services and prices:** the page is a "job tag" builder, like the paper tag a workshop writes for each bike. You pick a service package (£25 to £220) and extra jobs (puncture, hydraulic bleed, wheel true and others). A kraft-card tag beside the form adds up the labour price.
- **How to book:** a drop-off form that only accepts Tuesday to Saturday. It opens an email draft containing the job tag, with the phone number as a fallback, and there's a four-step "how booking works" section.

Run it through the site-prompt skill with Bash allowed if you want the build tested and replay-checked. Otherwise, open `index.html` in a browser before trusting it.
